title: What training is mandatory for employers in the UAE?
description: Mandatory employer training in the UAE by theme: safety, data, AML, financial services and health licensing, across federal, emirate and free zone rules.
shortAnswer: As at November 2026, mandatory training for employers in the United Arab Emirates depends on where an entity is licensed. Federal labor law requires training to avoid occupational risks, and federal anti money laundering law requires ongoing training plans. Abu Dhabi adds its own safety framework, the DIFC and ADGM set annual anti money laundering and cyber training, and Dubai and Abu Dhabi make annual CPD a condition of health license renewal.
keyTakeaways: The first question in the UAE is jurisdiction: federal onshore, an individual emirate, or a financial free zone such as the DIFC or ADGM. Each layer has its own regulators and training rules.

Fixed annual intervals appear mainly in free zone financial rules: ADGM requires anti money laundering training for all employees at least annually, and both the DFSA and ADGM require annual cyber training.
The federal Personal Data Protection Law names no training duty, while the DIFC and ADGM data protection laws make staff training part of the Data Protection Officer's monitoring role.
Health professional CPD in Dubai and Abu Dhabi is set by credits per year (40 for physicians and dentists, 20 for nurses and pharmacists, 10 for allied health), and missing it blocks license renewal.
Several instruments bind only some employers: the Information Assurance Regulation is mandatory for government and critical entities and voluntary for others.

sections.heading: How are mandatory training duties set in the UAE?

blocks.text: Mandatory training in the UAE comes from three layers that sit side by side: federal law that applies onshore, emirate level frameworks for matters such as occupational safety and health licensing, and the separate legal systems of the financial free zones. An employer's obligations depend on which of these layers its license falls under, so the same activity can carry different training rules in Abu Dhabi, in Dubai and inside a free zone.

The financial free zones are the clearest example. The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) has its own financial regulator, the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), and its own data protection law. The Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) was established under federal legislation and Abu Dhabi Law No. 4 of 2013, with a legal framework based on English common law ([ADGM](https://www.adgm.com/legal-framework)). The federal Personal Data Protection Law excludes free zone companies that have their own data protection legislation ([Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021, Article 2(2)](https://uaelegislation.gov.ae/en/legislations/1972)), so a DIFC or ADGM firm follows its zone's data law instead.

Some federal law reaches into the zones regardless. The DFSA states that federal anti money laundering legislation applies directly in the DIFC under Articles 70 and 71 of the Regulatory Law, with the DFSA as the competent authority for Relevant Persons ([DFSA](https://www.dfsa.ae/what-we-do/aml-ctf-sanctions-compliance/overview-of-dfsa-aml-ctf-sanctions-obligations)). A DIFC firm therefore trains to federal anti money laundering law and to the DFSA's own rulebook at the same time.

The tables below cover every UAE regulation page in this library, grouped by theme, as at November 2026. The library has no UAE pages on harassment or transport training, so those themes are not tabulated here. The [Australia](/guides/mandatory-workplace-training-in-australia) and [United States](/guides/mandatory-workplace-training-in-the-united-states) hubs show how much more of the workforce is covered by prescribed training in markets with longer statutory histories.

sections.heading: What health and safety training must employers provide?

blocks.text: Every private sector employer in the UAE must provide appropriate training to avoid occupational risks under Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 (Article 13), and in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi every place of employment is also covered by the Abu Dhabi Occupational Safety and Health System Framework (ADOSH-SF, formerly OSHAD-SF). How much training system an Abu Dhabi entity must run depends on the risk classification its sector regulatory authority assigns.

blocks.text: Two features of the Abu Dhabi framework shape a training plan. First, its codes of practice are mandatory for all entities regardless of risk classification ([ADPHC](https://www.adphc.gov.ae/en/Legislation/Code-of-Practices)), so a low risk office with outdoor workers still owes heat training. Second, the framework is versioned: Version 4.0 renamed OSHAD-SF to ADOSH-SF and replaced the OSHAD center name with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC), and several codes moved to Version 4.1 from 27 February 2026 ([ADPHC](https://www.adphc.gov.ae/en/Legislation/legislation-V4-updates)). Course materials that still cite OSHAD documents by their old version numbers need checking.

The heat code is one of the few UAE provisions with a calendar trigger. Code of Practice 11.0 requires heat training before work, in a language employees understand, within 10 days of starting employment and prior to the summer months ([CoP 11.0](https://www.adphc.gov.ae/-/media/Project/ADPHC/ADPHC/PDF/OSHAD-SF/Codes-of-Practise/11---Safety-in-the-Heat-v31-English.pdf)). For a seasonal workforce, that makes the onboarding window and the pre summer refresher the two dates the register must track.

sections.heading: What conduct and consumer protection training is required?

blocks.text: Conduct training in the UAE library is set by financial regulators rather than by general employment law. The Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) requires a code of conduct with regular training for its licensed institutions, and Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) requires an anti bribery and corruption training program for every board member and staff member of a licensed virtual asset service provider.

blocks.text: The CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards are binding in the same way as the regulation they implement ([CBUAE](https://rulebook.centralbank.ae/en/rulebook/consumer-protection-standards)). They go further than most conduct rules on evidence: Standard 3.2.1.5(d) asks for an annual evaluation of the effectiveness of frontline and control function competence, and Standards 5.1.1.49 to 5.1.1.61 require training records to be retained during employment and appraisal at least once a year. Complaint records are kept for five years (Standard 8.1.3.3(e)). An institution that can show attendance but not an evaluation of competence has met only part of the standard.

sections.heading: What privacy and information security training is required?

blocks.text: Privacy training duties differ by zone. The federal Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) requires appropriate technical and organizational measures but names no training duty, while the DIFC and ADGM data protection laws expressly include awareness raising and staff training in the Data Protection Officer's monitoring tasks. Information security awareness is mandatory for government and critical entities under the UAE Information Assurance Regulation.

blocks.text: The difference in penalties explains why free zone firms tend to document privacy training more formally. The DIFC law sets maximum fines of USD 25,000 for breaching the Article 14(1) compliance program duty and USD 50,000 for breaching the Article 14(2) measures duty ([DIFC Data Protection Law](https://www.difc.com/business/laws-and-regulations/legal-database/difc-laws/data-protection-law-difc-law-no-5-2020)). ADGM caps administrative fines at USD 28 million and treats technical and organizational measures as a factor in setting them ([ADGM DPR 2021, section 55](https://en.adgm.thomsonreuters.com/sites/default/files/net_file_store/ADGM1547_23167_VER992025.pdf)). Onshore, the PDPL leaves violations and penalties to a Cabinet decision (Article 26).

For the Information Assurance Regulation, the binding question is scope. Its National Information Assurance Framework makes compliance mandatory for all UAE government entities and entities identified as critical, and voluntary for others ([NIAF, section 1.5](https://assets.u.ae/api/public/content/4fdd52f9ff974ab0bf3e412183b4249c?v=8833f113)). Suppliers to those entities often receive the same controls through contract, so a private company can be bound in practice without being in scope by law. The regulation also measures awareness by the percentage of employees who participated in security awareness training (indicator for M4.3), which is a ready made register field.

sections.heading: What anti money laundering training does UAE law require?

blocks.text: Federal law requires financial institutions, designated non financial businesses and professions, and virtual asset service providers to run ongoing anti money laundering training for relevant employees, developed by a compliance officer at management level. The federal rules set no interval; the free zone regulators add their own, with ADGM requiring training for all employees at least annually.

blocks.text: The 2025 reforms replaced the federal framework that most existing UAE anti money laundering courses still cite. Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 repealed Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 (Article 41(1)), and Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 repealed Cabinet Resolution No. 10 of 2019 (Article 70) ([UAEFIU](https://www.uaefiu.gov.ae/media/3ssbp5d5/cabinet-134-2025.pdf)). The Cabinet resolution describes the compliance officer's duty as "developing, implementing and documenting ongoing programs and training plans for employees", which makes the training plan itself an evidence item a supervisor can ask for. Administrative fines run from AED 10,000 to AED 5,000,000 per violation ([Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025, Article 17](https://www.uaefiu.gov.ae/media/n5mflqwo/federal-decree-10-2025.pdf)).

blocks.title: Best practice is not regulation
blocks.text: The CBUAE's best practices on role based AML/CFT/CPF training describe an annual training needs assessment, board training at least annually with records, an annual content review and no credit without mastery, but the CBUAE states they are not additional regulation. They also cite the repealed 2018 decree-law as their legal basis. Treat them as the supervisor's view of good practice rather than as fixed intervals ([CBUAE](https://rulebook.centralbank.ae/en/rulebook/best-practices-licensed-financial-institutions-implementing-role-based-amlcftcpf-training)).

sections.heading: What competence and CPD rules apply to financial firms?

blocks.text: Financial firms in the two free zones must ensure their staff are fit and proper, competent, and trained in the zone's rules, and must show it with records. The DFSA adds a fixed CPD quota for key individuals, and both zones require annual cyber training for relevant employees.

blocks.text: The DFSA's scope changed in 2026. Amendments made by RMI 430 of 2025 took effect on 1 July 2026, and GEN 5.3.19 now applies to Relevant Employees rather than all Employees ([DFSA GEN 5.3.19](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/gen-5319)). DFSA guidance treats front office sales or trading and back office compliance or accounting as covered, and drivers, personal assistants and similar roles as ordinarily not. A DIFC register built before July 2026 may therefore over or under assign the competence population and is worth rechecking.

The DFSA CPD rule counts structured activities of thirty minutes or more toward the 15 hour quota and requires records ([GEN 5.3.19A](https://dfsaen.thomsonreuters.com/rulebook/gen-5319a)). Because the quota attaches to named controlled functions, the register should track it per person against the calendar year, not per course.

sections.heading: What training do healthcare employers have to track?

blocks.text: Healthcare professionals licensed in Dubai and Abu Dhabi must complete a minimum number of continuing professional development (CPD) credits each year to renew their license, set by a unified qualification standard issued jointly by the federal and emirate health regulators. Facilities employ the professionals and, in Dubai, share responsibility for compliance.

blocks.text: The annual minimums come from the Unified Healthcare Professional Qualification Requirements of April 2025, issued by the Ministry of Health and Prevention, DoH, DHA and the Sharjah Health Authority ([PQR, section 2.2](https://www.doh.gov.ae/-/media/D112FF75EF0140439A733B16081292DF.ashx)). The two emirates then differ on who carries the risk. The DHA manual makes failure to meet CPD a ground for rejecting renewal and suspending the right to practice, with penalties the joint responsibility of the professional and the facility ([DHA Manual, version 1.4](https://www.dha.gov.ae/attachments/regulatoryDocuments/1790949482460-374216735.pdf)). The DoH manual makes maintaining and submitting CME hours the professional's sole responsibility, while providers should ensure professionals obtain CME and keep written records ([DoH Healthcare Professionals Manual, sections 75.1 and 75.2](https://www.doh.gov.ae/-/media/A47D9907918943438EDB512BE9347AB8.ashx)).

Multi year licenses change the arithmetic. In Dubai, the CPD requirement is cumulative, so a physician on a three year license needs 120 credits, and credits cannot be carried forward into the next cycle. A facility that renews licenses within the three months before expiry, as the DHA manual expects, needs the professional's credit total well before that window opens.

sections.heading: What training do UAE schools and food businesses need?

sections.heading: How should a UAE employer build a single training register?

blocks.text: Build the register around legal entity and license first, then role, then instrument. In the UAE the same job title can carry different duties depending on whether the employing entity holds a CBUAE license onshore, a DFSA license in the DIFC, an FSRA permission in ADGM, or a VARA license in Dubai, so a register that starts from job titles alone will misapply rules.

items: **Map each entity to its jurisdictions.** Record the emirate, any free zone, and every regulator that licenses or supervises the entity. This decides whether the PDPL or a free zone data protection law applies, and which anti money laundering rulebook sits on top of federal law.

**List instruments per entity, with their binding status.** Mark which are binding (the decree-law, a rulebook rule, a code of practice) and which are guidance or best practice (CBUAE best practices, ADGM data protection guidance). Note the Information Assurance Regulation as binding only for government and critical entities, or by contract.

**Assign duties to roles and named people.** Some duties attach to everyone (ADGM annual AML training), some to defined populations (DFSA Relevant Employees), and some to named individuals (DFSA CPD for the SEO, Compliance Officer and MLRO; DPO knowledge).

**Record the frequency exactly as each source states it.** Keep annual intervals (ADGM AML, DFSA and ADGM cyber), credit quotas (DFSA 15 hours, health CPD), onboarding windows (VARA 30 calendar days, Abu Dhabi heat training within 10 days) and unspecified intervals (federal AML, DIFC data protection) distinct. Where no interval is set, record the risk rationale using the method in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

**Set retention per instrument.** The federal AML rules keep records five years, the DFSA and ADGM six years, and the CBUAE consumer protection standards for the duration of employment. Apply the longest rule that covers each record; see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

**Track source versions.** The 2025 federal AML reforms, the DFSA's July 2026 amendments and ADOSH-SF Version 4.x all changed citations in the past two years. Record the version each course was written against.

The [training matrix guide](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) covers the layout, and [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) covers the link between each obligation and the learning outcome that satisfies it.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each obligation against the entity, jurisdiction and source version it comes from, so a firm operating onshore and in a free zone can see which rule drives each learning outcome. When a source such as a rulebook or decree-law changes, the affected outcomes and roles can be identified rather than retraining everyone. The [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence) page describes how this evidence is held.

faqs.q: Does the UAE have a general legal requirement for annual compliance training?
faqs.a: No single law sets annual compliance training for all employers. Annual intervals appear in specific rulebooks: ADGM requires anti money laundering training for all employees at least annually, and both the DFSA and ADGM require annual cyber training for relevant employees. Federal anti money laundering law requires periodic and ongoing training without a fixed interval.

faqs.q: Does the federal PDPL apply to companies in the DIFC or ADGM?
faqs.a: Article 2(2) of the PDPL excludes free zone companies that have their own data protection legislation. The DIFC and ADGM both have their own data protection laws, which include staff awareness and training in the Data Protection Officer's monitoring tasks, so firms there train to the zone's law.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for a healthcare professional's CPD, the employee or the facility?
faqs.a: It depends on the emirate. The DHA manual in Dubai makes penalties for missed CPD the joint responsibility of the professional and the facility. The DoH manual in Abu Dhabi makes maintaining and submitting CME hours the professional's responsibility, while providers should ensure professionals obtain CME and keep written records.

faqs.q: Is the Information Assurance Regulation mandatory for private companies?
faqs.a: Only for entities identified as critical. The National Information Assurance Framework makes compliance mandatory for UAE government entities and critical entities and voluntary for others. Private suppliers may still be bound through contract terms with those entities.

faqs.q: How long should UAE training records be kept?
faqs.a: It varies by instrument. Federal anti money laundering rules require five years, the DFSA and ADGM rulebooks require six years for their training and competence records, and the CBUAE consumer protection standards require training records to be retained during employment. Apply the longest period that covers each record.

factCheck.claim: ADOSH-SF Element 1 s 3.2.5(b)(vii): information, instruction, training and supervision in appropriate languages; Element 5: TNA with ten minimum topics, risk based planning, evaluation, review of training requirements at least annually; Manual: applies to all places of employment in the Emirate (as recorded on oshad-abu-dhabi-ohs-training).

Codes of practice mandatory for all entities regardless of risk classification; several CoPs V4.1 effective 27 February 2026; Version 4.0 renamed OSHAD-SF to ADOSH-SF (as recorded on oshad-abu-dhabi-ohs-training).

CoP 11.0: heat training before work in a language employees understand, within 10 days of starting employment and prior to the summer months; Mechanism 5.0: five minimum topics and a training register for medium risk entities (as recorded on oshad-abu-dhabi-ohs-training).
Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 Article 41(1) repeals Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018; Article 17(1)(b) fines AED 10,000 to AED 5,000,000 per violation (as recorded on uae-aml-cft-training-requirements).

Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 Article 21(5) periodic anti-crime programs and workshops; Article 22 compliance officer duty to develop, implement and document ongoing programs and training plans for employees; Article 25 five year retention; Article 70 repeals Cabinet Resolution No. 10 of 2019 (as recorded on uae-aml-cft-training-requirements).

CBUAE best practices on role-based AML/CFT/CPF training: annual TNA, board training at least annually, annual content review, no credit without mastery; not additional regulation; cites Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 (as recorded on uae-aml-cft-training-requirements).

DFSA: federal AML legislation applies directly in the DIFC under Articles 70 and 71 of the Regulatory Law; DFSA is competent authority (as recorded on dfsa-training-and-competence-requirements and uae-aml-cft-training-requirements).

DFSA GEN 5.3.19 amended by RMI430/2025 effective 1 July 2026 to Relevant Employees; GEN 5.3.19A 15 hours CPD per calendar year for SEO, Compliance Officer and MLRO via structured activities of thirty minutes or more; GEN 7.7.1 annual review; GEN 7.7.3 six year records; GEN 5.5.14 annual cyber training; AML 12.1.1 appropriate and regular intervals; GEN 4.3.1 guidance on covered roles (as recorded on dfsa-training-and-competence-requirements).

ADGM FSRA AML 13.2.1 AML/TFS training for all Employees at least annually; AML 13.3.2 records at least six years; GEN 3.5.13 cyber training at least annually; GEN 3.3.19 fit and proper, competent and trained (as recorded on adgm-fsra-training-and-competence).

VARA Rules I.J: training at beginning of employment and ongoing, AML/CFT training on a regular basis, operational policies communicated within first 30 calendar days; VI.D anti-bribery and corruption training for Board and all Staff, induction; I.C.2(a) and III.A.2(a) CO and MLRO training responsibilities (as recorded on vara-staff-training-requirements).

CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards mandatory and enforceable; 3.2.1.5(d) annual evaluation of effectiveness; 5.1.1.49 to 5.1.1.61 People of Determination training, ongoing professional development, records retained during employment, appraisal at least once a year; 8.1.3.3(e) five year complaint record retention (as recorded on uae-central-bank-consumer-protection-training).

PDPL Article 2(2) exclusions including free zone companies with own data protection legislation; Article 7(1) and 7(4); Article 10 DPO; Article 26 penalties by Cabinet decision; no executive regulations listed (portal checked 28 Sep 2026) (as recorded on uae-pdpl-staff-training).

DIFC DP Law Article 18(3)(a)(iii) DPO monitors awareness-raising and training; Article 14; Article 16(2) DPO mandatory for DIFC Bodies and High Risk Processing; Schedule 2 fines USD 25,000 (Art 14(1)) and USD 50,000 (Art 14(2)) (as recorded on difc-data-protection-law-training).

ADGM DPR 2021 s 37(1)(b) DPO awareness-raising and training; s 43(2)(l) BCR training; s 55(1) fines capped at USD 28 million, s 55(3)(d) measures a factor; ODP guidance Part 5 example of joiner training plus annual refresher (as recorded on adgm-data-protection-training).
ADGM established under federal legislation and Abu Dhabi Law No. 4 of 2013 with a legal framework based on English common law (as recorded on adgm-data-protection-training).

UAE IA Regulation M3.3.1 P1 Always Applicable, M3.2.1 sub-controls, omission of Always Applicable controls is non-conformity, M4.3.1 policy on first access, M4.3 indicator percentage of employees in Security Awareness Training; NIAF s 1.5 mandatory for government and critical entities, voluntary for others (as recorded on uae-information-assurance-awareness-training).

PQR April 2025 s 2.2 annual CME/CPD minimums: physicians and dentists 40, nurses 20, pharmacists 20, allied health 10, TCIM 10 (as recorded on dha-cpd-requirements-dubai and doh-abu-dhabi-cme-requirements).

DHA Manual v1.4: cumulative CPD for multi year licenses (120 for a 3 year physician license); facility applies within three months of expiry; failure results in rejection and suspension of right to practice; penalties joint responsibility of professional and facility; 70 percent specialty and 30 percent general; no carry forward (as recorded on dha-cpd-requirements-dubai).

DoH Healthcare Professionals Manual s 75.1 professional's sole responsibility to maintain and submit CME hours; s 75.2 providers should ensure professionals obtain CME and keep written records; DoH CPD Standard minimum 50 percent formal per licensure cycle, 1 hour = 1 credit (as recorded on doh-abu-dhabi-cme-requirements).

Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 Article 13(5) to (7) appropriate training to avoid occupational risks and periodic evaluation; Cabinet Resolution No. 1 of 2022 Article 4(3)(c) juvenile training (as recorded on uae-federal-osh-employer-training-duties).

DFSA GEN 5.4.2 written whistleblowing policies with periodic review (as recorded on difc-whistleblowing-requirements); AI Ethics Guide personnel education (as recorded on uae-ai-governance-guidance-for-organizations); CBUAE broker Article 5.3 training courses, Article 2.16 one year license (as recorded on uae-cbuae-insurance-sector-staff-competence); KHDA induction topics before teaching (as recorded on khda-dubai-school-child-protection-training); ADEK policies induction and mandated training (as recorded on adek-abu-dhabi-teacher-licensing-and-safeguarding); Dubai Food Code 3.1.1 PIC certificate valid five years, 6.2 handlers trained (as recorded on dubai-municipality-person-in-charge-food-safety); Abu Dhabi Decree 6 of 2020 Article 3(c) (as recorded on abu-dhabi-food-handler-training-requirements).
